newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin retreats from view, health doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin retreats from view, health doubts remain.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin retreated from view again on Wednesday after a brief television appearance which failed to dispel all doubts about his recovery from double pneumonia.

The Kremlin, repeating a phrase used often since Yeltsin dropped out of sight last July with heart problems, said the president would work on documents at the Gorky-9 country residence outside Moscow.
It said he was not expected to return to the Kremlin during the day.
Yeltsin went to the Kremlin on Tuesday, his second visit since he went down with pneumonia on January 8. He looked alert and animated in television footage of the visit.
But he appeared to have lost a lot of weight over the past few weeks and the film was heavily edited and without sound, making his true condition hard to gauge.
The television clip was shown as speculation in the Russian press about the Kremlin's pronouncements on Yeltsin, who had not been seen since January 6, reached fever pitch.
"Boris Yeltsin's appearance in the Kremlin dispelled rumours of an empty presidential motorcade shuttling between the Kremlin and Gorky," the newspaper Sevodnya said.

But a series of cancelled meetings -- Yeltsin had been due to chair a much-postponed summit of leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States on Wednesday and visit the Hague next week -- kept some observers worried about his ability to rule.

Yeltsin, who turns 66 on Saturday, had two heart attacks in 1995 and spent six months out of the Kremlin last year before and after multiple bypass surgery, from which he was still recovering when the pneumonia struck.
The liberal opposition daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta said his poor health and the Kremlin's attempts to put a brave face on it had taken their toll on foreign policy.

"It was precisely last year, when Yeltsin began to adopt the practice of non-appearances at international forums because of his health, which marked the start of a period of deterioration in relations between Russia and the West," the paper said.

"A lack of foreign visits by the president is a minus for Russia. But even worse are annoucements that the visits are about to take place. The West is beginning to think that it is being taken for a ride and stop believing Russia," it said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday that he had no reason to believe that the Kremlin was misleading Washington over Yeltsin's health and that a summit would go ahead in March as planned.
But U.S. officials said health concerns meant it might be held in a third country rather than in Washington.

On doctors' orders Yeltsin on Monday cancelled a trip to the Netherlands to meet the president of the European Union next week. But the Kremlin said a meeting with French President Jacques Chirac would go ahead on Sunday near Moscow.
The Kremlin leader's busy international agenda is focused on trying to reach an agreement on the thorny, and increasingly pressing, issue of NATO's planned expansion to the East.
The defence alliance is expected to issue invitations to some of Moscow's former communist allies in July but is a long way from overcoming Russia's objections.

But Yeltsin is also trying to keep up the policy momentum closer to home. The Kremlin said he had spoken by telephone with Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko on Wednesday and discussed meeting next month to boost integration between the neighbouring states.
